## Quick refresher

[Playground](https://playground.tensorflow.org/)

![](playground_2.png)

::: {.notes}
Things that we will need to discuss about the playground should come here.
There are four parts to this UI
the top bar has the play button to start the fitting, next to it we see how many epochs or training rounds the fitting has gone for, 
Next to it we have a set of hyper parameters like the learning rate, the activation etc. but we are not going to touch on that today

The left most panel contains the datasets that we can use for this demonstration, we will use this one for ease of understanding

The middle panel shows the layers and the flow of data in the model. We can add up to 8 neurons in a hidden layer. For this demonstration I will use four neurons. We can add more layers if needed but for simplicity in this case let's use one hidden layer. and then on the right hand we have the fit of the model on the entire xy plane. we get to see the training and testing loss and we get to see the testing dataset on the plane as well.

We can start fitting a model by pressing the play button and after we are happy with the result we can add or remove more neurons, we can restart the training etc. Give it a try and see how it feels for 3 minutes. 
:::

## Fitting a neural network

- It looks easy, right? We'd like to hit an easy button to get a model!
- Most of the time, we care only about the performance of the model and the modeling pipeline.
- Given the computational power we have, we rarely care about the size or complexity of the models.
- _If it predicts well all is ok, right?_

# Fitting our own neural network

## Let's work on fitting this dataset 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=60%}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 100%
dataset <- arrow::read_parquet(
  "train_df.parquet.lz4"
)

original_bound <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  "[[-10,-10],[-8.875,-3.75],[-4.21875,-3.75],[-0.3125,1.25],[5,-5],[10,10]]"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  setNames(c("x", "y"))

p <- ggplot(dataset, aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(class))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  geom_line(
    data = original_bound,
    aes(x = x, y = y),
    linewidth = 2,
    alpha = 0.5,
    color = "white",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(color = "Class", x = "x", y = "y") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text = element_blank())
p
```

:::
::: {.column width=30%}

<br><br>
This has two predictors, `x`, `y` and 

one response, `Class`, a categorical variable with two levels. 

:::
::::

## Hyperparameters

**These hyperparameters are fixed for now**

- Number of epochs: 100
- Batch size: 71
- Loss function: Binary Cross Entropy loss
- Optimizer: Adam
- Training set size: 5,000
- Testing set size: 5,000

## What have we learned? {.smaller}

:::{.incremental}
- The role of a neuron in a neural network is to define a linear hyperplane (a "cut") that partitions the input space.
- More neurons do not always result in better performance in training and testing set
- The random seed has an effect on a model's performance
- Larger neural networks tend to have more consistent performance on multiple metrics.
- Smaller neural networks can be as performant as the larger one
    - but they tend to vary (depending on the initial random seed)
- Always fit your neural networks with differing seeds to see what the effect is on the model.
:::

:::{.fragemnt}
On a separate note,

- Ask why and how things work, or do something different from what we expect
- The big black boxes of neural networks are not so dark with little glimmers of light

:::
